title: Messages in certain large public Discord servers will be searchable on the web after December
summary: Discord is attempting to solve the 'this should've been a forum' problem with specially-designated channels whose messages can show up in search engines.
body: What once would've been a forum or wiki is often now a Discord server, and that's created a problem : valuable information is hidden away deep in the chat logs of big public Discord channels, rather than in easy-to-search forum pages on the web. Discord now aims to solve that problem by making discussions in some of its biggest public servers searchable on the web. The change will only apply to "Discoverable Servers," which refers to certain large public Discord servers with 1,000 or more users. The admins of those specially-designated servers will be able to opt out of search engine discoverability, and individual users can also opt out of allowing their messages in those servers to be searchable on the web. The change does not affect any invite-only servers or DMs. "Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios," reads a blog post from Discord. body: Recently, I travelled to Guildford, England, to interview developer Peter Molyneux, the legendary game developer behind Populous, Theme Park, Dungeon Keeper, Black & White and Fable, among others. And, as part of that interview, which covered everything from Molyneux's brand-new god game, Masters of Albion , which has just got a huge game-changing update , through the moment he conceptualized Black & White's famous titan creatures , and onto the bombshell news that a Black & White remaster could be incoming , I also asked the father of the god game genre about AI use in the video game industry. body: As AI continues to get smarter, the schemes using it have often become more successful. Despite allegedly obtaining 8.2 million records and demanding 360,000,000 Won (around $271.77K) from victims, the gang is said to have ended up receiving 300,000 Won (around $210). This is according to Yonhap News Agency , Seoul Economic Daily , and The Chosun Daily , which corroborate reports. Altogether, the gang reportedly accessed files from over 90 firms, but 60 successful hits came from hacks using AI tools (a mixture of AI coding and an autonomous penetration testing system). The stolen data is said to have included customer information like names, registration numbers, phone numbers, and addresses. The cyberhacking gang is also said to have sent threatening emails to those affected, saying, "If the data breach becomes public, the company’s reputation will be damaged, and government fines may be imposed."
